strengths: The proposed approach REEF is training-free, simple and efficient.
The proposed approach REEF does not impair the model’s general capabilities.
The proposed approach REEF is robust to sequential fine-tuning, pruning, model merging, and permutations.

The proposed approach REEF is intuitive as feature representations of fine-tuned victim models are similar to feature representations of the original victim model, while the feature representations of unrelated models exhibit distinct distributions.

Experimental evaluation considers an informed adversary who is aware of the proposed approach REEF and tries to evade detection, creating that adversary through the designing of a customized loss function that maximises the representational divergence between models; results in Appendix D indicate that such fine-tuning seriously damages the model’s general capabilities and renders the fine-tuned models unusable.
Experimental evaluation considers comparison with baselines: Weight-based Fingerprinting Methods and Representation-based Fingerprinting Methods.
Experimental evaluation considers robustness to fine-tuning, pruning, merging, permutation and scaling transformation.

This paper appears to be original, taking the known idea that models develop distinct feature representations, and introducing a novel use of the central kernel alignment score to measure similarity between these representations robustly; the scheme does not require changing the training algorithm of the original model, which is a nice property.

This paper is clearly written and well organized; the experiments are comprehensive in comparing the REEF scores of several known models, considering various practical attacks, and also compare REEF to several existing fingerprinting schemes.
The result appears to be a significant incremental improvement; REEF is a slightly more robust fingerprinting scheme than existing schemes, with solid practical improvement.
Protection of the IP of the large language model is an urgent and important topic.
The experiments are extensive to show the effectiveness of the proposed method.
The authors clearly identify the challenges and limitations of existing fingerprint methods.
The paper is well-organized and easy to follow.
The proposed method identifies descendant models of a large language model through kernel-based similarity with the original model, allowing for robust and effective discovery of descendant models.
The method is intuitive and well-supported by analytical study.
weaknesses: This paper creates that adversary by designing a customized loss function that maximises the representational divergence between models; it is unclear if a more effective way to create such an informed adversary exists, such as designing a better loss function or performing other operations.

The paper studies the impact of sample numbers on the performance of REEF but provides no evaluation of the type of data points for a given number of samples; it is unknown whether performance could improve with specific sample selection rather than random sampling.
The paper considers only one single family of LLMs as a victim model; generalization of results to other families of victim models would be interesting.

One observation is that "CKA from a single layer is sufficient for fingerprint identification"; it is unclear how detection performance degrades if only the last layer is used, which would relax the assumption of requiring access to intermediate representations.

REEF does not offer any provable false positive guarantee, and the work does not measure the false positive rate; the sample size is insufficient to extrapolate a false positive rate in general, raising concerns about accusations of model theft.
It is unclear how REEF would perform on two models that are independently trained on similar datasets; such a scenario could lead REEF to incorrectly assert that one model is stolen from the other.
It would be interesting to see what happens when a model is fine-tuned to minimize its REEF score with the model it is derived from.
The novelty is limited in replacing similarity measures of prior work.
There is a lack of theoretical analysis of the proposed methods.

The first heatmap of Figure 6 shows that two LLMs trained on different datasets have a high CKA similarity, which would lead REEF to classify them into the same model; this suggests that all models using the same architecture but trained on different datasets would share the same fingerprint, which is problematic.

The security model and fingerprint verification setting are not clearly defined; the method is only effective in a white-box scenario where parameters of both descendant and original models are publicly accessible, and the paper lacks detail on the verifier’s capabilities and available information.

The proposed fingerprint verification method is limited to direct descendant models of the original “root” model and is not designed for verifying claims from these descendants against further generations, a significant limitation for real-world scenarios with multiple stages of fine‑tuning or adaptation.
